newsitem.title: UK: Few surprises in UK windfall tax, IFS says.
newsitem.headline: Few surprises in UK windfall tax, IFS says.

text.p: Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown's windfall tax on the privatised utilities yielded few surprises and the threat of legal action from afflicted companies may have receded, the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said on Thursday.
Brown, in his first budget speech, said the tax would raise 5.2 billion pounds with 400 million off from a reduction in the North Sea Gas levy.

The water and regional electricity companies bear the brunt of the tax, with British Telecom having to pay 500 million stg and BG and Centrica, the two offshoots off British Gas, stumping up a little more than 700 million.

"I think Brown is probably right. The tax won't really hit employment, prices or the quality of service," said Lucy Chennels of the IFS. "It's a one-off tax based on past profits not the future." She said the fact that BT was having to pay out less than many economists expected may have reduced the threat of legal action on the government.
"We will have to wait and see of course, but legal challenges seem fairly unlikely especially now BT, which had probably the base case, is paying less than expected."
But she added that it will be shareholders that will count the cost of the tax and not necessarily those who netted the excess gains.
